title: What is the Deloitte consulting interview process, and how should you prepare?
description: How Deloitte consulting hires, including Monitor Deloitte: online assessments, video interviews, case and group exercises, and the free official practice…
hook: Deloitte's consulting process depends on the country and the part of Deloitte you apply to, but it usually combines an online assessment or screening stage with behavioural interviews, case interviews and, in some routes, a group exercise. Deloitte is the largest of the Big Four by revenue and hires a great many graduates and experienced professionals each year. The first step is knowing exactly which Deloitte, and which role, you are applying to.
body:
In this guide

  • Know which Deloitte you are applying to
  • The UK early-careers process
  • The US consulting process
  • How Deloitte wants you to approach a case
  • A worked example: one problem, three roles
  • How to prepare
  • Common mistakes
  • Practice
  • Where to go next

Know which Deloitte you are applying to

Deloitte reported $70.5B of revenue for fiscal 2025 and $74.5B for fiscal 2026, with more than 500,000 people. It operates through member firms that largely run their own recruiting, so a UK graduate process and a US experienced-hire process can look quite different.

Within consulting, the role matters as much as the country. Strategy work sits under the Monitor Deloitte brand, built on Monitor Group, which Deloitte acquired in 2013. Other consulting roles cover technology, operations, human capital and more, and the type of case you get depends on the group. If you are interviewing for Monitor Deloitte or another strategy role, prepare as you would for MBB. For technology or operations roles, expect cases with more emphasis on process, systems and delivery.

The UK early-careers process

For its main UK early-careers routes, Deloitte's assessment guidance describes five stages, as of 2026:

  1. Online application.
  2. Immersive online assessment: behavioural scenarios plus cognitive questions on numerical and verbal reasoning.
  3. Job simulation: work-based tasks such as ranking options, written answers and recorded video responses.
  4. Final-stage assessment: two exercises, a topic discussion with an assessor followed by a skills and motivation interview. It is usually in person; Deloitte says it is virtual for summer vacation scheme applicants.
  5. Outcome.

For entry-level apprentices and some shorter programmes, Deloitte combines stages two and three into a single online assessment called OneStop. Always follow your own invitation.

The US consulting process

Deloitte US publishes free case interview preparation for entry-level consulting roles (and a separate scenario-interview tool for audit and assurance). Prep guides describe US consulting hiring as organised around practice groups such as Strategy and Operations (which includes Monitor Deloitte), Technology and Human Capital.

For experienced hires, guides describe a first round pairing a behavioural interview with one or two case interviews, and a final round that adds a group case, usually with a partner involved. In a group case, a handful of candidates review the same materials, discuss them while interviewers observe, then answer questions. How to stand out in a group case.

Deloitte's cases are generally candidate-led, and you may occasionally receive written materials to review before the discussion starts.

How Deloitte wants you to approach a case

Deloitte's own case interview guidance sets out a five-step approach:

  1. Clarify the issue, asking questions as needed.
  2. Identify the assumptions behind the case.
  3. Summarise the key issues and findings.
  4. State your recommendations.
  5. Outline next steps and expected impact.

Its recruiters stress that the interview is not about finding one right answer but about how you think and respond under pressure. Their tips: take notes, make sure you understand the question before analysing, ask clarifying questions without using them as a crutch, share a framework and an initial hypothesis, explain your reasoning out loud, and treat the interview as a business conversation.

A worked example: one problem, three roles

Prompt: A manufacturer ships 100,000 orders a year. Its average fulfilment cost has risen 20%, from $12 to $14.40 per order. What is going on? (Illustrative numbers.)

Size it first. Old cost: 100,000 × $12 = $1.2M. New cost: 100,000 × $14.40 = $1.44M. The increase is $240k a year, if volume is unchanged.

Diagnose. Standard orders cost $10 to fulfil and urgent orders $30. The data shows urgent orders rose from 10% to 22% of the total.

  • Old average: 90% × $10 + 10% × $30 = $9 + $3 = $12.00.
  • New average: 78% × $10 + 22% × $30 = $7.80 + $6.60 = $14.40.

So the whole increase comes from the mix shift towards urgent orders, not from any rise in unit costs. Now the role shapes the next question:

  • Strategy: should the company change its customer promise, for example charge for urgent delivery?
  • Operations: why are urgent orders rising? Poor demand forecasting by customers, or sales staff promising speed by default?
  • Technology: does the order system make "urgent" the default option, or fail to show stock availability, prompting rush orders?

A strong recommendation, whichever role:

"The $240k increase is entirely the shift to urgent orders, from 10% to 22%. Automating the warehouse would not fix that. I'd introduce a fee for urgent delivery and review how the order system presents delivery options, then track the urgent share monthly."

To size the fee idea: there are 100,000 × 22% = 22,000 urgent orders. If a $15 fee made half of those customers switch to standard, the company would save 11,000 × ($30 − $10) = $220k and collect 11,000 × $15 = $165k in fees from the rest.

A weak answer jumps to "invest in automation" without sizing or diagnosing. The maths here is simple, but it tells you which workstream matters.

How to prepare

  • Use Deloitte's free case interview practice tool. Deloitte says it is not an assessment and does not track your answers, so you can repeat cases as often as you like.
  • Read its case interview tips page and practise the five-step approach out loud.
  • Practise timed numerical and verbal reasoning for online assessments.
  • Practise short, clear recorded video answers if your route includes them.
  • Prepare competency stories, such as teamwork, adapting to change and delivering under pressure, alongside cases. Common fit questions lists what to expect.
  • Practise a group case with friends if your process includes one.

Common mistakes

  • Preparing for the wrong Deloitte. Ask your recruiter which business you are interviewing for and which exercises are planned.
  • Assuming every role has a case. Some routes rely on online assessments, simulations and behavioural interviews instead.
  • Skipping the "next steps" step. Deloitte's own approach ends with next steps and expected impact. Finish there.
  • Dominating the group case. Interviewers watch how you work with others, not just what you know.

Practice

1. In the fulfilment case, what urgent share would bring the average cost back to $12?

Show the answer

Each percentage point of urgent orders adds $0.20 to the average ($30 − $10 = $20, times 1%). At 10% urgent the average is $10 + 10 × $0.20 = $12. So the urgent share must fall back to 10%.

2. Which group case behaviour helps you most: giving the most ideas, or summarising where the group has got to?

Show the answer

Usually summarising. A well-timed summary ("So we agree the main driver is urgent orders; shall we look at options?") shows structure and leadership and helps the group, while a stream of ideas can look like you are competing rather than collaborating. Contribute ideas too, but make them build on others'.

Where to go next

Read how Big Four consulting compares with MBB, then continue with PwC and Strategy&. Sharpen the weighted-average maths from this example with weighted averages.
